question_text: Classify the oxide CO₂ as neutral, acidic, basic or amphoteric.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Carbonic acid and the litmus colour
lines: Carbon dioxide CO₂ is an acidic oxide.
It dissolves in water and gives a weak
So moist blue litmus paper turns red.
Carbon here is in its higher state, +4.
steps.why: Carbon dioxide is the anhydride of carbonic acid, and the litmus colour is the same fact in visible form. Carbon follows the usual pattern of a non-metal: the higher oxide, with the element in the higher oxidation state, is the acidic one.
common_mistakes: Calling CO₂ neutral because it is a gas. The physical state of an oxide has nothing to do with its class.
Writing H₂CO₃ as a strong acid. Carbonic acid is weak, and most of the dissolved gas stays as CO₂.
steps.memory_tip: CO₂ plus water gives carbonic acid, so moist blue litmus turns red.
steps.margin_note: The water equation and the litmus colour state the same acidic character.

steps.label: Carbonate then bicarbonate

lines.text: CO₂ is acidic: it gives carbonic acid

lines: With an alkali it gives a salt and water,
which is what an acidic oxide does:
Passing more CO₂ into that solution gives
steps.why: Carbon dioxide gives two different salts with the same alkali, and which one forms depends on how much gas is passed in: a limited amount gives the carbonate, and an excess turns that carbonate into the bicarbonate. Sodium bicarbonate is the less soluble of the two salts, so it separates out of the solution.
common_mistakes: Writing one NaOH and still writing Na₂CO₃: the salt has two sodium atoms, so two NaOH are used.
Giving NaHCO₃ as the product with a limited amount of CO₂. The carbonate forms first; the bicarbonate needs an excess of the gas.
steps.memory_tip: A little CO₂ gives the carbonate, more CO₂ gives the bicarbonate.
steps.margin_note: The alkali equation is the direct answer here; the bicarbonate line follows from it.

insider_note: Carbon dioxide is the acidic oxide of carbon and carbon monoxide is the neutral one, so name the oxide before you name the class. The equation with an alkali is stronger evidence than the litmus colour alone.
